content: A general practitioner (GP) is a medical doctor who provides primary care and specializes in family medicine. They manage both acute and chronic illnesses, offer preventive care, and provide health education for individuals of all ages and genders. GPs are particularly skilled in treating patients with multiple health issues and comorbidities. The term general practitioner is commonly used in countries like Ireland, the United Kingdom, some Commonwealth nations, and Bulgaria. In English-speaking countries, the term physician is often reserved for specialists in fields like internal medicine. In the UK, a Principal GP is a senior doctor, similar to an attending physician in other systems, and typically holds a Certificate of Completion of Training in general practice. GPs may also care for hospitalized patients if they have hospital privileges, and they may perform minor surgeries or obstetric procedures. Many GPs conduct minor procedures, such as removing skin lesions, in their offices. Historically, GPs performed more major surgeries, such as tonsillectomies and hernia repairs, especially in rural areas, where this practice still persists. However, the rise of medical specialists in recent decades has led to a decline in the number of family physicians worldwide. In Brazil, general practice is referred to as clínica geral or clínica médica. Physicians can legally practice without additional training after graduating from medical school, but there are efforts to require a specialist title for general practice, similar to other specialties like cardiology or endocrinology. Most Brazilian GPs work in the public health sector and are often young, recently graduated doctors. General practice is not highly profitable, leading many doctors to pursue specialized training. Family medicine has recently emerged as a distinct specialization in Brazil, influenced by community health models from Europe and Cuba. The Family Health Program (Programa de Saúde da Família or PSF) was introduced to address issues in primary healthcare, initially facing challenges but later expanding significantly. The PSF now involves multidisciplinary teams, including physicians, nurses, dentists, and community health agents, and is one of the largest family health programs globally. In Canada, there are no newly qualifying general practitioners; all medical students pursue a specialty, with family medicine accounting for nearly 40% of residency positions. After four years of medical school, residents spend 2-3 years in an accredited family medicine program and can then take the Certification in the College of Family Physicians of Canada (CCFP) exam. Many family physicians add extra training in areas like emergency medicine, anesthesia, or surgery. Most family physicians in Canada are remunerated through provincial government health plans, with payment models including fee-for-service, salaried positions, and alternate payment plans. Rural family physicians often provide a broad scope of practice, and efforts are underway to address manpower inequities in these areas. In the United States, family medicine is recognized as a medical specialty. Family physicians complete undergraduate education, medical school, and a three-year residency in family medicine. They are board-certified and must maintain certification through ongoing education and periodic exams. Many family physicians deliver babies and care for patients of all ages. The average starting salary for family physicians in the U.S. ranges from $120,000 to $150,000 annually. There is a growing trend toward micro-practices, which reduce overhead costs and allow physicians to spend more time with patients, improving satisfaction for both parties. In Australia, general practice training requires completion of a medical degree (traditionally a six-year MBBS program or a four-year graduate program), followed by a oneor two-year internship. Doctors then enter a three-year Australian General Practice Training Program, leading to the Fellowship of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (FRACGP). Since 1996, this qualification has been required to access Medicare rebates as a GP. There is a shortage of GPs in rural and outer metropolitan areas, leading to the recruitment of overseas-trained doctors. In India, medical graduates earn an MBBS degree after a six-year program, followed by a one-year internship. They can then practice as GPs or pursue postgraduate training in specialties like internal medicine. Family medicine is a relatively new specialty in India, with fellowship programs available through the National Board of Examinations. Graduates of alternative medical systems like homeopathy and Ayurveda can also practice as family practitioners if registered with the appropriate boards. In Pakistan, medical graduates complete a five-year MBBS program and a one-year internship before receiving permanent registration from the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC). They can then practice as GPs or pursue specialty training. Family medicine training programs were introduced in the 1990s, and some are recognized by international bodies like the Royal College of General Practitioners in the UK. In France, the médecin généraliste provides long-term care, including prevention, education, and management of diseases and traumas that do not require a specialist. They also handle legal responsibilities, such as issuing medical certificates and participating in emergency care. Training includes six years of medical school, followed by a two-and-a-half-year internship, culminating in a doctorate. In the Netherlands and Belgium, general practice is advanced, with GPs (huisarts) providing first-line care and referrals. Training involves three years of specialization in the Netherlands and two years in Belgium. In Spain, family physicians work in multidisciplinary teams at primary care centers. After a six-year medical degree, doctors complete a four-year residency in family and community medicine. Some Spanish family physicians work abroad due to limited job opportunities in the public health system. In the UK, GPs undergo at least four years of training after medical school, which includes two years of foundation training and two years in a General Practice Vocational Training Scheme. Since 2008, new GPs must complete the Membership of the Royal College of General Practitioners (MRCGP) qualification. Most GPs work under the National Health Service (NHS), with income derived from contractual arrangements. Visits to GP surgeries are free in the UK, though prescription charges vary by region.
